subject: Medicine
summary: Hepatomegaly is an enlarged liver seen in many infections, metabolic and cardiac conditions. Clinicians must link history, exam and simple tests to identify the underlying cause and avoid life‑threatening complications.

sections.p: Hepatomegaly is a palpable liver edge below the costal margin. In low‑resource settings, a simple abdominal palpation and percussion are the mainstays.
b: Palpable edge >2 cm below costal margin

t.b: Measures actual size; normal <15 cm in adults
Identify hepatocellular injury, cholestasis or biliary obstruction
Detect anaemia, thrombocytopenia indicating hypersplenism or portal hypertension

sections.p: Severity is graded by size and associated symptoms. In resource‑poor settings, clinical staging (mild, moderate, severe) guides urgency.
b: Mild: 1–2 cm below margin, no symptoms
Moderate: 3–5 cm, mild pain, early ascites
Severe: >5 cm, marked pain, ascites, encephalopathy

sections.p: In East Africa, infections dominate. Causes are grouped by organ system and epidemiology.
b: Infectious: malaria (hepatomegaly with splenomegaly), schistosomiasis, HIV hepatitis B/C, tuberculosis
Metabolic: sickle cell disease, glycogen storage disease

t.b: Detect malaria parasites or sickle cells

t.a: Serology for hepatitis B surface antigen

sections.p: Patients may be asymptomatic or have pain, nausea, jaundice, or systemic signs of infection.
b: Right upper quadrant pain, nausea, vomiting
Ascites, pedal oedema, raised JVP in cardiac causes

t.b: Look for jaundice, spider naevi, ascites, peripheral oedema

sections.p: Prioritize tests that are affordable and available. When unavailable, clinical judgment must guide management.

t.b: Low albumin suggests chronic liver disease

sections.p: Certain features mandate urgent referral or admission.
Treat the underlying cause first, then support organ function. Drug choices consider local availability and safety.
b: Infections: antimalarials, anti‑TB therapy, antiretrovirals, hepatitis B therapy (tenofovir)
Cirrhosis: lactulose for encephalopathy, beta‑blockers for varices
Malignancy: referral for oncology, palliative care

t.b: Avoid NSAIDs due to renal risk

sections.p: Regular monitoring of liver size, function tests and symptom progression is essential. Prevention focuses on infection control and safe practices.
b: Screening for malaria in endemic areas

sections.p: Several conditions mimic hepatomegaly; distinguishing them is key.
b: Right pleural effusion (dullness on left side)

sections.p: Some tests may be falsely normal or abnormal in low‑resource settings.
b: Serum bilirubin may be normal in early hepatitis
Ultrasound may miss small lesions if operator inexperienced

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly enlarging liver, severe pain, vomiting blood, jaundice with confusion, tense ascites, INR >1.5

faq.q: What is the most common infectious cause of hepatomegaly in East Africa?
faq.a: Malaria, especially in children, often presents with hepatomegaly and splenomegaly.

faq.q: How do you differentiate hepatomegaly from splenomegaly on exam?
faq.a: Hepatomegaly is felt below the right costal margin; splenomegaly is felt in the left upper quadrant, often with a palpable splenic tip.

faq.q: Why is ultrasound not always available, and what can you do instead?
faq.a: Ultrasound requires equipment and trained staff; in its absence, rely on clinical exam, basic labs and symptom history.

exam: A 7‑year‑old boy from a malaria‑endemic area presents with fever, abdominal pain and a palpable liver edge 4 cm below the costal margin. What is the first investigation? — Peripheral blood smear for malaria parasites.
A 45‑year‑old woman with chronic hepatitis B has a liver span of 18 cm and mild ascites. What is the next step in management? — Start tenofovir and monitor LFTs.
A patient with right‑heart failure shows hepatomegaly and pedal oedema. Which drug should be avoided and why? — NSAIDs, because they worsen renal function and fluid retention.
A child with hepatomegaly and jaundice has a normal bilirubin level. What could explain this? — Early hepatitis B/C infection before bilirubin rises.
An elderly man has a dull percussion note over the right flank and a palpable liver edge 6 cm below the margin. What is the most likely diagnosis? — Cirrhosis with portal hypertension.
A patient presents with sudden severe abdominal pain and a rapidly enlarging liver. What is the red flag? — Rapid enlargement >5 cm and pain suggests hepatic rupture or infarction.
related: Sickle cell disease and hepatic sequestration
